claims.text: Slower reduction kinetics promote more uniform atomic mixing in noble metal-based HEA nanomaterials.
Enhanced configurational-entropy effects are responsible for the more uniform atomic mixing under slower reduction.
More uniform atomic mixing leads to formation of a single-phase alloy.
A single-phase, uniformly mixed alloy has better catalytic performance than material produced by fast, uncontrolled reduction.
The initial precursor state is a mixed high-entropy solid solution.
Rapid synthesis can kinetically limit atomic mixing.
Reduction rate can be controlled by comparing slow dropwise precursor addition with fast, uncontrolled reduction while holding other synthesis conditions constant.
Slower reduction conditions involve reduced atomic mobility at lower temperatures.
Reduced atomic mobility allows configurational entropy to homogenize the elemental distribution more effectively.
A homogeneous elemental distribution produces a single-phase HEA.
Uniform elemental distribution produces a consistent distribution of catalytic active sites.
A consistent distribution of catalytic active sites leads to higher catalytic efficiency.
Slowly reduced HEA nanomaterials will display a single homogeneous phase relative to the fast-reduction baseline.
Slowly reduced HEA nanomaterials will exhibit higher conversion rates or turnover frequencies than the fast-reduction baseline.
X-ray diffraction and X-ray absorption spectroscopy can assess phase purity and atomic distribution in the synthesized nanoparticles.
Failure of slow reduction to produce statistically significant improvements in both structure and catalytic performance would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The controlled comparison states that synthesis conditions other than reduction rate are identical, but the mechanism attributes slow reduction to lower temperature and reduced atomic mobility. Temperature therefore appears both fixed and mechanistically changed.

The initial state is described as a mixed high-entropy solid solution, while formation of a homogeneous, single-phase alloy is treated as the synthesis-dependent mediator. This makes it unclear whether the homogeneous solid solution already exists before the intervention or is its intended product.
